name: Opal glass: white light-scattering glass, cased or flashed on clear
summary: Glass made milky white by a second phase dispersed through it (historically tin or arsenic oxide, bone ash, cryolite or fluorspar) that scatters light almost ideally in every direction. In the museum it is always a thin opal layer carried on clear glass: cased in mouth-blown globes (Albion's electroliers, the Reserve's pendants, the grounds' lamp standards) and flashed on drawn sheet (the Salon's bay-2 lantern, the Reserve's picture-light lenses).

formation.how: An opal glass is melted with an opacifier that stays dissolved while the glass is hot and separates as it cools into tiny particles (or droplets) of a different refractive index; each particle scatters, and many together send light out in all directions, so the glass glows evenly and hides the lamp. A solid opal glass would absorb and back-scatter too much, so the trade carries a thin opal layer on clear glass: flashed on a drawn or blown sheet, or cased in a blown globe between clear layers.

opacifiers.text: Opacity is produced by 'oxide of tin, oxide of arsenic, phosphate of lime, cryolite or a mixture of felspar and fluorspar'.
opacifiers.source: H. J. Powell, W. Rosenhain and A. Nesbitt, 'Glass', Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), via Wikisource, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Glass

construction.text: OPALIKA is 'a colourless base glass which serves as a carrier material and a thin white flashed layer for producing a diffuse and shadow reducing light'.
construction.source: SCHOTT North America, 'OPALIKA' technical data sheet (970-3d/09/04-P), https://www.sydor.com/wp-content/uploads/SCHOTT-OPALIKA-Display-Glass.pdf

casedConstruction.text: Triplex: 'A thin opal layer is sandwiched in between two outer layers of clear glass'; the hand-blown inner clear form is overlaid with opal, then with clear.
casedConstruction.source: Arlico Lighting, 'Lucis: hand made opal glass lighting', https://arlico.co.uk/brands/lucis-hand-made-opal-glass-lighting/

optics.kind: volume scatterer (thin layer) on a clear dielectric carrier

globeLuminance.text: 600 + 5400 cos^7 nits core to rim, averaging 1800 nits over the disc for a 3400 lm lamp in a 17-inch ball; 'Opal is never even: milky clouds (6 cm) and a slower drift (18 cm)', +/-9 % and +/-6 %.

opalGlobeEmissive.text: M_OpalGlobe: an unlit emissive of colour (1.0, 0.82, 0.62) at 2500 nits.

asBuiltCorrection.text: The as-built globes are emissive surfaces with hand-set nits. Physically a globe's luminance is the lamp's flux through the opal: transmitted flux about 0.3 (flashed) to 0.5-0.55 (conventional cased) of the lamp's lumens, spread nearly Lambertian over the globe, plus the thin direct 'nose'. Light should derive the glow from the lamp and this record, not from a nits constant.
asBuiltCorrection.source: MuseeVision/Journal/Decisions.md, D-001 (the design is the finished museum) and D-017 (port the finished rooms; the as-built material values seed the records)

photograph: A lit opal globe is brightest where the view passes nearest the lamp and falls off to the rim, faintly warmer at the rim; the lamp itself is not visible, only perhaps a soft brighter core.
The cased skin is glossy: it mirrors the room and the other lamps; unlit, the globe is a soft milky white with a slightly bluish cast in daylight.
Hand-blown opal is never perfectly even: faint clouds and a denser neck.

evidenceSearch.tier: The data sheet's spectrum and diffusion indicatrix carry the physics; a photographed lit globe would be a tier-(b) reference for Studio.

unverified.reason: The diffuse reflectance of flashed opal was not read. By analogy with a white fired frit of the same transmittance (T 0.32, R 0.57-0.62, Wilson and Elstner 2018) it is probably near 0.6, but that is a different material.
The transmittance of the museum's cased globes depends on the opal layer's thickness, which a maker would set; the 0.50-0.55 figure is a manufacturer's claim for 'conventional' opal glass shades.
Modern opal glasses are said to use fluoride or phosphate opacifiers (fluoride crystals such as NaF or CaF2); not read from a primary source.
